questions.q: Why doesn't Theo treat a successful kubectl rollout status as proof the incident is resolved?
options: Because kubectl rollout status is always inaccurate
Because a clean rollout confirms the change is live, not that the underlying imbalance is actually fixed under real traffic
Because rollouts take more than a day to finish on AKS
Because the Deployment needs to be deleted and recreated to confirm anything
questions.explain: A rollout completing is a deployment-mechanics checkpoint; Theo still needs to confirm, with real data, that the fix actually resolved the per-zone imbalance under live load.

questions.q: What does the second per-zone pod listing show after the fix is applied?
options: All twelve pods are now in a single zone
Four pods in each of the three zones — matching what maxSkew: 1 across 3 zones and 12 replicas was designed to produce
The pods have been reduced to six total
The pods are now running in a fourth, new availability zone
questions.explain: Four pods per zone is the even distribution the topology spread constraint from Lesson 13 guarantees.

questions.q: What do the per-zone CPU numbers look like after the fix, compared to before?
options: One zone is still at 96% while the others are idle
All three zones sit close together, roughly 46-48%, with no zone saturated and none idle
All zones are now at 100% CPU
CPU utilization cannot be measured per zone
questions.explain: With pods evenly spread, the sale's real traffic load is now distributed across the capacity that was always there — no zone saturated, none idle.

questions.q: What is the real proof Theo relies on to confirm the fix worked, beyond the pod listing?
options: The FinOps dashboard's cluster-wide average, unchanged
The reliability dashboard — the same one that caught the original spike — returning to its baseline p95 latency (~190ms) and error rate (~0.2%) while the sale's traffic is still live
A text message from Casey Lindqvist saying it's fine
The absence of any error logs in the terminal
questions.explain: The dashboard that originally caught the problem returning to baseline, under continuing live traffic, is the direct evidence the fix resolved the actual customer-facing issue.

questions.q: Why does Theo keep both dashboards open for the rest of the sale instead of closing the incident as soon as latency drops?
options: Because closing an incident requires a 24-hour waiting period by policy
Because a fix holding for twenty minutes and a fix holding through the rest of the sale's traffic ramp are different claims, and only the latter is worth reporting as resolved
Because the FinOps dashboard needs to be rebuilt first
Because Casey Lindqvist has not yet approved the fix
questions.explain: Validation under sustained real load is a stronger claim than a brief post-fix check, and it's the claim Theo wants to be able to make honestly to leadership.
